dm: Abandoning all other thoughts, With a mind focused only on myself, I shall strive to settle the mind in meditative equipoise And to bring it under discipline.
gm: Having abandoned all other thoughts, With a single-pointed intention, In order to settle the mind in equipoise And to subdue it, I shall strive.

dm: In this world and in the next, Desires produce ruin; Here, they lead to being killed, bound, and mutilated, And in the next, they bring about the hells and so forth.
gm: In this world and in the next, Desires produce ruin: Here, killing, bondage, and amputation, And in the next, establishing hells and so forth.

dm: For whose sake you previously employed male and female messengers, And for whose sake you did not shrink from even sin or infamy, And for whose sake you disregarded everything,
gm: Previously through male and female messengers, For whose sake I made many requests, And regarding sins or ill repute, For whose sake I did not hesitate;

dm: Entering into dangers and exhausting your wealth— Those very things that you embrace with such supreme delight Are nothing other than skeletons;
gm: I also entered into danger, And exhausted my wealth; By fully embracing whom I was supremely delighted—those very ones

dm: If they are nothing but skeletons and nothing else, And are neither independent nor a self, Why, after desiring them intensely and becoming thoroughly attached, Do you not go to the state beyond sorrow?
gm: Are nothing but skeletons, nothing else. Being neither independent nor a self, Strongly desiring and fully clinging to them, Why do you not proceed to nirvāṇa?

dm: That which you first exerted yourself to lift, And which looked down bashfully even when drawn up— Whether it was seen before or not, That face was covered by a cloth.
gm: Which at first was lifted up with effort, And though drawn near, looked down out of modesty; Whether seen before or unseen, Whose face was covered by a cloth;

dm: That face of your affliction, Is now revealed just as it is; Now that you see it being uncovered by the vultures, Why do you flee from it?
gm: That face which tormented you, Just as it has now become manifest, Having seen it unveiled by vultures, Why do you flee from it now?

dm: Even when others merely looked with their eyes, You kept it thoroughly guarded; While it is being devoured by them, Why, O miser, do you not protect it?
gm: Even when others looked at it with their eyes, It was completely guarded; Now that it is being eaten by them, Miser, why do you not guard it?

dm: Seeing this heap of flesh being eaten by vultures and others, Why do you honor the food of others with flower garlands, Sandalwood, and ornaments?
gm: Seeing this heap of flesh, When vultures and others eat it, Why do you offer to the food of others Garlands of flowers, sandalwood, and ornaments?

dm: Seeing it as nothing but a heap of bones, If you are terrified even when it is motionless, Why are you not afraid when it is moved by someone, Like a reanimated corpse?
gm: Having seen it as merely a heap of bones, If you are terrified even when it does not move, When it was moved by something, like a zombie, Why were you not afraid?

dm: Since both excrement and saliva arise from the very same food, Why do you dislike the excrement, And yet, why do you delight in the saliva?
gm: From a single food alone, If feces and saliva are produced, Out of these, you dislike the feces, So why do you delight in the saliva?

dm: Instead of taking delight in a pillow, Which is soft to the touch like cotton, The lustful are deluded regarding the impure, Claiming, "It does not leak a foul odor."
gm: Of cotton, which is soft to the touch, You do not delight in a pillow, Saying it does not emit a foul odor; The lustful are deluded by filth.

dm: Since you are attached to this when it is covered, Why do you not desire it when it is uncovered? If you have no need for it then, Why do you embrace it when it is covered?
gm: If you are attached to it even when covered, Why do you not desire it when uncovered? If you have no need for it uncovered, Why do you embrace it when covered?

dm: If you have no attachment to what is impure, Why do you embrace in your lap another, A cage of bones bound together by sinews, And plastered over with the mud of flesh?
gm: If you have no attachment to filth, To a cage of bones tied together with sinews And plastered with the mud of flesh, Why do you embrace another in your lap?

dm: You yourself contain plenty of filth, And you constantly wallow in that; Yet, out of a craving for the impure, You also desire other bags of filth.
gm: You yourself contain much filth, Which you continually make use of, Yet for other bags of filth as well, Out of a craving for filth, you desire them.

dm: If you say, "I am fond of this flesh," And desire to touch and look at it, Then why do you not desire flesh In its natural, insentient state?
gm: Saying, "I delight in this flesh," If you desire to touch and look at it, Which is of a mindless nature, How can you desire the flesh?

dm: That mind which you desire Cannot be touched or seen, And that which can be touched is not consciousness; What is the use of such a meaningless embrace?
gm: That mind which you desire Cannot be touched or seen, And whatever can be is not conscious; What is the point of a meaningless embrace?

dm: It is not so wonderful that you do not realize The foul nature of another's body; But that you do not realize your own very self To be foul is truly a great wonder.
gm: That another's body is of an unclean nature, Not realizing this is not so amazing; That you yourself are filth itself, Not realizing this is truly amazing!

dm: Having abandoned the young lotus Opened by the rays of a cloudless sun, Why does your mind, with its attachment to the impure, Take delight in a cage of filth?
gm: Opened by the rays of a cloudless sun, Abandoning a fresh lotus, With a mind attached to filth, Why do you delight in a cage of filth?

dm: If you do not wish to touch a patch of ground Because it is soiled with filth, How can you wish to touch the body From which that very filth arose?
gm: A place smeared with filth, If you do not wish to touch, From which that filth arose, How can you wish to touch the body?

dm: If you have no attachment to what is impure, Then why do you embrace in your lap another Who was produced by that seed And arose from an impure field?
gm: If you have no attachment to filth, Arisen from a field of filth, And generated by its seed, Why do you embrace another in your lap?

dm: You do not desire even a tiny worm That arises from filth, Yet you desire a body that is a mass of many impurities And was likewise born from filth.
gm: A filth-worm arisen from filth, Even a tiny one, you do not desire, Yet a body whose nature is much filth, And born of filth, you desire.

dm: Not only do you not feel revulsion For your own impurity, But out of a craving for filth, You also desire other bags of impurity.
gm: Towards your own filth, Not only do you not disparage it, But out of craving for filth, You desire another bag of filth.

dm: Even pleasant things like camphor, Or boiled rice and vegetables, Once taken into the mouth and spat out, Make even the ground foul and unclean.
gm: Even pleasing things like camphor, Or cooked rice and vegetables, If put into the mouth and spat out, Make even the ground foul and filthy.

dm: If you still have doubts about such impurity, Even though it is plainly evident, Then observe other impure bodies Abandoned in the charnel grounds.
gm: If such filth as this Is obvious, yet you doubt it, The bodies discarded in the charnel grounds, Look at that other filth as well.

dm: If you know that great terror would arise If the skin were peeled back, Then how could you ever again Find pleasure in that very same thing?
gm: If the skin is peeled away from it, Great fear will arise; Knowing this, how can you Feel joy in that very thing again?

dm: Even the fragrance applied to the body Is that of sandalwood and the like, not of anything else. Why then do you become attached to one thing Because of the fragrance of another?
gm: That scent smeared on the body Is sandalwood and so forth, nothing else; Because of that scent of another thing, Why are you attached to another?

dm: If it is naturally foul-smelling, Is it not better to be unattached to it? Why do those with meaningless worldly cravings Anoint it with sweet scents?
gm: If its nature is foul-smelling, Is it not better to not be attached to it? Those who pointlessly burn with craving in the world, Why do they smear it with sweet scents?

dm: If the fragrance is that of sandalwood, What part of it comes from the body? Why then do you become attached to one thing Because of the fragrance of another?
gm: If the sweet scent belongs to sandalwood, What does that have to do with the body here? Because of the scent of another thing, Why are you attached to another?

dm: If the body’s natural state—with its long hair and nails, Yellowish teeth, and the stench of mud— Is a terrifying sight when left naked, Why do you take such pains to polish it?
gm: If long hair and nails, Yellowish teeth, and a foul, muddy smell, Imbue the nature of the body, And make it terrifying indeed when naked,

dm: Why do you groom it so zealously, As if it were a weapon that will only harm you? Through the efforts of those deluded regarding the self, The entire earth is thrown into turmoil by the mad.
gm: Like a weapon that harms oneself, Why make efforts to clean and polish it? Through efforts driven by self-delusion, This earth is thoroughly agitated by madmen.

dm: If you feel revulsion in a charnel ground Upon seeing nothing but a heap of bones, Why do you delight in the "city charnel ground," Which is filled with moving skeletons?
gm: Having seen just a skeleton, If you feel disgust in the charnel ground, Pervaded by moving skeletons, Are you delighted by the charnel ground of the city?

dm: That which has become so impure Cannot be obtained for free; By striving for its sake, one suffers exhaustion And is harmed by the torments of hell and the like.
gm: That which has thus become filthy, Cannot be obtained without a price; Exhaustion from accomplishing that goal, And harm in hells and so forth will follow.

dm: Since a child is unable to increase wealth, What happiness is there when one reaches one's prime? If one's life is exhausted by the accumulation of wealth, Once old, what is the use of sensual desires?
gm: Since as a child one cannot amass wealth, When coming of age, what happiness is there in this? If life is exhausted by amassing wealth, What can be done with desires in old age?

dm: Some wretched, lustful people, Utterly exhausted by a long day's work, Return home and lay their weary bodies Down to sleep like corpses.
gm: Some miserable people with desires, Utterly exhausted by the day's work, Come home with worn-out bodies, And sleep exactly like corpses.

dm: Some are afflicted by the hardships of travel And the suffering of going far away; Though they long for their wives and children, They do not see them for years on end.
gm: Some suffer the afflictions of traveling abroad, And the misery of going far away; Although longing for their wives and children, They do not see them for years on end.

dm: Deluded by the desire for their own benefit, They sell themselves for the sake of profit; Yet without attaining it, they are meaningless, Driven by the winds of others' labor.
gm: Utterly deluded about what benefits themselves, Even selling themselves for that very purpose, They do not obtain it, and uselessly Are driven by the wind of others' work.

dm: Some sell their own bodies And, powerless, are put to work by others; Even when their wives give birth, It happens in the wilderness or at the foot of a tree.
gm: Some sell their own bodies, And powerlessly become employed by others; Even when their wives give birth to children, They are simply born at the foot of trees in the wilderness.
